item.dc:creator: Emmanuel Okogba
item.content:encoded: Last week, I started a discussion of General Yakubu Gowon’s multi-themed memoirs, My Life of Duty & Allegiance. My focus was on the book’s general tone, which I find unduly self-justificatory. In his attempts to defend his legacy, General Gowon presents himself as a saintly figure who did no wrong as a leader, whereas some introspection and nuanced reflection would have helped. That said, the book is a treasure trove of insightful details that enrich our historical narrative. This week, I will focus on one of such insights, namely, the quality of governance and public service ethos under General Gowon’s regime, with Chief Obafemi Awolowo singled out as the arrowhead of a remarkable governance approach that, if replicated today, would transform how Nigeria is governed and, thus, this country’s fortunes. As a political economist and policy practitioner who spent nearly 20 years advising the UK government on diverse policy areas, in addition to teaching public policy, I have professional and intellectual interests in how government is run. Thus, I was enthralled by General Gowon’s fascinating accounts of how the affairs of state were conducted under his administration, with the triumvirate of politicians (as ministers), civil servants (as technocrats), and universities and think-tanks (as sounding boards) driving policy formulation and implementation and setting standards of good and effective governance. Sitting atop the triumvirate was Chief Awolowo, an extraordinarily transformative leader! Indeed, if General Gowon’s memoirs can be said to have a hero, that hero is Chief Obafemi Awolowo, appointed by Gowon as the Vice Chairman of the Federal Executive Council, FEC, and Commissioner of Finance in his administration. In every reference to Chief Awolowo in the memoirs, General Gowon writes glowingly and superlatively about him. Gowon also gives credit to his colleagues in the Supreme Military Council, SMC, and the first-class mandarins who ran the civil service for his administration’s successes, especially its ability to prosecute a 30-month civil war “without endangering the national economy”. But he reserves his most generous praise for Chief Awolowo. Hear Gowon: “Chief Awolowo’s business acumen, political sagacity, economic wizardry and thorough man-management ability would later prove quite useful and helpful in ensuring that we kept our finances intact during and immediately after the civil war that broke out a few weeks after his appointment to the FEC.” He adds: “Without any argument, he made invaluable contributions.” Of course, Chief Awolowo’s reputation preceded him. As the premier of the Western Region, he performed so superbly that Harold Wilson, then British prime minister, described him as a “world-class leader”, who would make an outstanding President of America or Prime Minister of Britain. General Gowon himself referenced Chief Awolowo’s pedigree, saying that he appointed him as the Commissioner of Finance with concurrent responsibility as Vice-Chairman of the FEC “because of his experience in politics and management of the economy of the old Western Region.” Indeed, General Gowon was so enamoured of Chief Awolowo that he admits in his memoirs that one of his administration’s flagship policies, the Universal Primary Education, UPE, was based on a policy introduced by Chief Awolowo as premier. “In scope and content,” Gowon writes, “UPE was not radically different from the model that was initiated by Chief Awolowo in the defunct Western Region while he was the Premier.” Two lessons emerge from this narrative. First, good leaders get the brightest and best in their teams; they form what a British prime minister described as GOATs (“Government of All the Talents”). Second, good leaders embrace good ideas and best practices worldwide. Indeed, one of the universally recognised approaches to sound policymaking is international comparison, which allows a government to consider what works elsewhere. Sadly, neither lesson is embedded in governance in Nigeria today. For instance, today, a Nigerian leader would fill his cabinet with cronies and political jobbers rather than seasoned technocrats and brilliant administrators. There’s also the phenomenon of policy discontinuities. Virtually every government won’t complete projects started by its predecessor, let alone copy sensible policies elsewhere, resulting in widespread abandoned projects and policy failures. But there’s another unlearned lesson. Chief Awolowo was never a yes-man in General Gowon’s government. Gowon himself cites two instances to prove this. In both instances, General Gowon eventually had his way, but Awolowo laid down the marker. In one case, General Gowon procured the services of a Lebanese contractor for the government. But Chief Awolowo refused to approve payment to the contractor, arguing that “the process of getting help from the Lebanese was not properly followed and documented and, as such, was an extra-budgetary expenditure.” Tell me, how many extra-budgetary expenditures are waived through without due process today? Can a finance minister challenge a president’s frivolous spending today? In another case, Chief Awolowo refused to approve a request for additional money for Gowon’s upkeep after the original budget was exhausted. He argued that the possibility of overshoots should have been considered before the budget was prepared and approved. This is how Gowon puts it in his memoirs: “Everyone knew how difficult it was to get anything out of Chief Awolowo without well-reasoned arguments.” What an extraordinary testimonial! But where are such principled and painstakingly meticulous ministers and public officers in Nigeria today? Sadly, none! To be sure, a tree does not make a forest, and Chief Awolowo did not act alone. As premier of the Western Region and later as Commissioner for Finance and Vice Chairman of the FEC, Chief Awolowo was surrounded by outstanding colleagues and civil servants. For instance, General Gowon mentions the sterling role of Professor Adebayo Adedeji, the world-renowned economist, who was the Commissioner for Economic Development. And talking about bureaucrats, who can forget the “Super Perm Secs” of the Gowon era? As the German sociologist and political economist Max Weber put it, “the state will not conduct its affairs without the bureaucracy.” Oxbridge-educated mandarins like Ahmed Joda, Allison Ayida and Philip Asiodu led what Gowon describes as “the deeply cerebral, committed and efficient technocrats in the civil service”, which he calls “the engine room” of his government. But where are today’s “super perm secs”? Where is today’s vibrant and technocratic civil service? Sadly, today, Nigeria has one of the worst civil services in the world, a subject I discuss in my book, In The National Interest, arguing that the collapse of the civil service and the public sector in general is at the heart of Nigeria’s acutely weak state capacity. As a scholar-practitioner, I was also excited about General Gowon’s accounts of how his government worked closely with universities. He writes: “We made exceptionally effective use of the many eggheads that populated the various university campuses to shape the policy directions.” He adds: “Many of the dons at the university were our formal and informal sounding boards for policy formulations and analyses.” In the UK, the government works in tandem with universities and think-tanks to shape policies. Sadly, in Nigeria, the government is anti-intellectual, with academics and think-tanks ostracised and treated as pariahs, rarely engaged in policy development. General Gowon makes another profound point about the policy process, saying: “These policies were not unilateral decisions. We diligently thought through the policies, and we implemented them based on their overall benefits to the people.” Compare that with how President Tinubu impulsively removed the fuel subsidy after he was “possessed by courage”,

item.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5063-5069 Rocks and Chips
item.description: Curiosity Navigation Curiosity Home Mission Overview Where is Curiosity? Mission Updates Science Overview Instruments Highlights Exploration Goals News and Features Multimedia Curiosity Raw Images Images Videos Audio Mosaics More Resources Mars Missions Mars Perseverance Rover Mars Curiosity Rover Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter Mars Odyssey More Mars Missions Mars Home 2 min read Curiosity Blog, Sols 5063-5069 Rocks and Chips NASA’s Mars rover Curiosity acquired this image of chip-shaped crystal forms using its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI), located on the turret at the end of the rover’s robotic arm, on November 7, 2026, Sol 5067 of the Mars Science Laboratory Mission, at 14:07:35 UTC. NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS Written by William Farrand, Senior Research Scientist, Space Science Institute Earth planning date: Friday, Nov. 6, 2026 This week Curiosity has been completing its drill campaign at the “Nazca” drill hole. This is an area characterized by bedrock containing disk-shaped (or in a liberal interpretation, potato chip shaped … see linked image) crystal forms. A key objective has been to better characterize these chip-shaped features. Drill samples were delivered to the Sample Analysis for Mars (SAM) instrument. While the SAM analysis was on-going, Monday’s plan included a ChemCam LIBS observation of another crystal-form, “Ahi Veremos,” more Mastcam frames to fill out a mosaic of the Nazca near to mid-field, and environmental observations including a large dust devil survey, and horizon and atmospheric zenith movies. Wednesday’s plan included two targeted science blocks with a LIBS depth profile of the “Colca” crystal-form and LIBS of the “Bermejo ” target. A long distance Remote Micro-Imager (RMI) mosaic of rock clusters below the “Cordillera” ridge was also collected. Mastcam collected more frames of its Nazca mosaic, and more environmental observations were made. Friday’s planning was for three sols with three targeted science blocks and a drive away from the Nazca drill site. A MAHLI mosaic of the side of the block that hosts the Nazca drill hole was planned. It was also planned to use MAHLI’s nighttime white-light and ultraviolet LED lamps for nighttime imaging of the crystal-forms. Mars’ moon, Phobos, was eclipsing the Sun and imaging of that event was prioritized. ChemCam LIBS observations were planned for each sol including a cluster of crystal forms, a resistant layer in the side of the Nazca block and a dark float rock. A long distance RMI mosaic of dark lenses beneath a planar surface on the “Mishe Mokwa” ridge was to be made. Another round of environmental observation was also planned. Finally, Friday’s drive was to take the rover back towards its southerly trending route where Curiosity would continue its trek of exploration and discovery. A long distance RMI mosaic of dark lenses beneath a planar surface on the “Mishe Mokwa” ridge was to be made. Another round of environmental observation was also planned. Finally, Friday’s drive was to take the rover back towards its southerly trending route where Curiosity would continue its trek of exploration and discovery. item.title: The US built world’s greatest card system
item.description: By YVONNE-FAITH ELAIGWU The history of payments is, in many ways, the history of making value easier to move. We started at barter and are now at electronic transfers, with stablecoins suggesting that the next evolution is here. New payment methods rarely make their predecessors useless. Cash did not immediately eliminate barter. Cards did not eliminate cheques. Account-to-account payments will not eliminate cards. But payments evolve. And one of the most interesting examples of that evolution can be found in an unlikely comparison: Nigeria and the United States. The United States built perhaps the world’s greatest card ecosystem. Nigeria just seems to have built past it. The American card system is extraordinary. Over decades, the U.S. built an ecosystem connecting consumers, merchants, issuing banks, acquiring banks, and card networks. Around it grew credit bureaus, credit scores, revolving credit, chargebacks, fraud protection, loyalty points, airline miles, and billions of dollars of rewards. Consequently, Americans have a compelling reason to use cards. And use them, they do. Data from the Federal Reserve show that credit-card payments reached 67.1 billion transactions in 2024, while ACH processed an enormous $104.06 trillion in 2024. America, therefore, doesn’t lack account-to-account infrastructure. The difference is where A2A sits in everyday consumer behaviour. Walk into an American store, and the natural question is still: Which card am I using? In Nigeria, increasingly, a different question is asked: “What is your account number?” That difference is more significant than it appears. Nigeria took another road. Nigeria never developed America’s deep credit-card culture. Debit cards became widespread, but cards did not become as deeply embedded in the country’s economic architecture as they did in America. Instead, Nigeria increasingly solved digital payments at the bank-account level. At the centre of this transformation is the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System and its NIBSS Instant Payment platform, built to operate 24/7 with most transactions settling in under one second. This infrastructure changed behaviour. Any individual or company can pay another individual or merchant, and the transaction can be executed on a Friday evening or a Sunday morning. The expectation is still remarkably simple: the money should arrive now. That expectation is one of Nigeria’s greatest payment achievements. America’s success may be part of its problem. This is where the comparison becomes fascinating. America isn’t stuck on cards because it cannot build something better. It may be stuck on cards partly because cards work so well. The merchant already has the terminal. The consumer already has the card. The bank earns card revenue. Visa and Mastercard provide enormous networks. item.content:encoded: By YVONNE-FAITH ELAIGWU The history of payments is, in many ways, the history of making value easier to move. We started at barter and are now at electronic transfers, with stablecoins suggesting that the next evolution is here. New payment methods rarely make their predecessors useless. Cash did not immediately eliminate barter. Cards did not eliminate cheques. Account-to-account payments will not eliminate cards. But payments evolve. And one of the most interesting examples of that evolution can be found in an unlikely comparison: Nigeria and the United States. The United States built perhaps the world’s greatest card ecosystem. Nigeria just seems to have built past it. The American card system is extraordinary. Over decades, the U.S. built an ecosystem connecting consumers, merchants, issuing banks, acquiring banks, and card networks. Around it grew credit bureaus, credit scores, revolving credit, chargebacks, fraud protection, loyalty points, airline miles, and billions of dollars of rewards. Consequently, Americans have a compelling reason to use cards. And use them, they do. Data from the Federal Reserve show that credit-card payments reached 67.1 billion transactions in 2024, while ACH processed an enormous $104.06 trillion in 2024. America, therefore, doesn’t lack account-to-account infrastructure. The difference is where A2A sits in everyday consumer behaviour. Walk into an American store, and the natural question is still: Which card am I using? In Nigeria, increasingly, a different question is asked: “What is your account number?” That difference is more significant than it appears. Nigeria took another road. Nigeria never developed America’s deep credit-card culture. Debit cards became widespread, but cards did not become as deeply embedded in the country’s economic architecture as they did in America. Instead, Nigeria increasingly solved digital payments at the bank-account level. At the centre of this transformation is the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System and its NIBSS Instant Payment platform, built to operate 24/7 with most transactions settling in under one second. This infrastructure changed behaviour. Any individual or company can pay another individual or merchant, and the transaction can be executed on a Friday evening or a Sunday morning. The expectation is still remarkably simple: the money should arrive now. That expectation is one of Nigeria’s greatest payment achievements. America’s success may be part of its problem. This is where the comparison becomes fascinating. America isn’t stuck on cards because it cannot build something better. It may be stuck on cards partly because cards work so well. The merchant already has the terminal. The consumer already has the card. The bank earns card revenue. Visa and Mastercard provide enormous networks. Consumers receive points, miles, fraud protection, and access to credit. Everyone has something to lose from changing the system. Even the Federal Reserve has acknowledged the economic tension. The better yesterday’s infrastructure becomes, the harder tomorrow’s infrastructure can be to adopt. Nigeria had a different incentive. Nigeria faced different circumstances. Card payments existed, but the country had stronger incentives to develop alternative digital rails. Rather than building everything around the card, Nigeria created interoperable infrastructure allowing value to move directly between accounts. The result is not perfect. Instant payments introduce their own fraud problems. So, this is not an argument that cards are bad. Cheques aren’t bad either. They are simply technologies belonging to particular stages in the evolution of payments. America is catching up. The United States has recognized the need for real-time payments. The Clearing House launched RTP in 2017, and in July 2023, the Federal Reserve launched FedNow, allowing participating financial institutions to transfer funds in near real time, 24/7/365. The rails now exist. The challenge is making instant A2A payments as culturally normal at the American checkout as tapping a credit card. Nigeria has already crossed much of that behavioural bridge. It has also established formal Open Banking guidelines. There is a broader lesson here: technological development isn’t always linear. Sometimes, developing countries do not follow developed countries through every generation of infrastructure. They skip one. America perfected the card. Nigeria had less reason to protect it. And that may have made it easier to build what comes after it. *Elaigwu is an experienced operations leader with a background in financial services and corporate social responsibility. She is currently Head of Operations at OnePipe, where she drives customer experience and governance. The post The US built world’s greatest card system appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: 2027 Elections: Beyond INEC, 375 Judges’ integrity under trial
item.description: By Ikechukwu Nnochiri With the 2027 general elections just 65 days away, all eyes are on the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to conduct a smooth, free, fair, and credible poll. Meanwhile, preparations for the aftermath are already under way. A total of 375 judges have been nominated to serve on election petition tribunals, where they will adjudicate disputes brought by candidates and parties dissatisfied with the results. The judges, drawn from courts across the federation, were inaugurated on Monday, November 9, at a ceremony held at the Body of Benchers Complex in Abuja. Similarly, section 134(3)(a) and (b) of the Electoral Act, 2026, prescribes the timelines for constituting the tribunals and opening their registries. The swearing-in, organised by the President of the Court of Appeal, Justice Monica Dongban-Mensem, marked the formal assumption of a responsibility with considerable constitutional, professional and public significance. A three-day intensive workshop followed immediately. It was designed to deepen the judges’ knowledge of the Electoral Act 2026, familiarise them with applicable practice directions and the evolving jurisprudence of the courts on election-related cases, and sharpen the practical skills needed for case management, evaluation of evidence, control of proceedings, and the delivery of clear, well-reasoned judgments within the prescribed timelines. item.dc:creator: Nwafor
item.content:encoded: By Ikechukwu Nnochiri With the 2027 general elections just 65 days away, all eyes are on the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to conduct a smooth, free, fair, and credible poll. Meanwhile, preparations for the aftermath are already under way. A total of 375 judges have been nominated to serve on election petition tribunals, where they will adjudicate disputes brought by candidates and parties dissatisfied with the results. The judges, drawn from courts across the federation, were inaugurated on Monday, November 9, at a ceremony held at the Body of Benchers Complex in Abuja. Section 285(1) and (2) of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, vests in the President of the Court of Appeal the responsibility for constituting election petition tribunals to adjudicate disputes arising from National and State Houses of Assembly and governorship elections. Similarly, section 134(3)(a) and (b) of the Electoral Act, 2026, prescribes the timelines for constituting the tribunals and opening their registries. The swearing-in, organised by the President of the Court of Appeal, Justice Monica Dongban-Mensem, marked the formal assumption of a responsibility with considerable constitutional, professional and public significance. A three-day intensive workshop followed immediately. It was designed to deepen the judges’ knowledge of the Electoral Act 2026, familiarise them with applicable practice directions and the evolving jurisprudence of the courts on election-related cases, and sharpen the practical skills needed for case management, evaluation of evidence, control of proceedings, and the delivery of clear, well-reasoned judgments within the prescribed timelines. The CJN also used the occasion to launch the second edition of the Judicial Electoral Manual (JEM), which she said will help judicial officers locate relevant authorities, appreciate the development of the law and approach recurring issues with greater clarity. According to the CJN, by bringing together the relevant constitutional provisions, the Electoral Act 2026, applicable practice directions and judicial decisions, the Manual provides a useful resource for judicial officers and other stakeholders in the electoral adjudicatory process. She was quick to warn, however, that it should serve only as a guide and a reference tool. It does not replace independent judicial reasoning or relieve any judicial officer of the duty to consider each case on its own facts, the arguments of counsel and the applicable law. The Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, Prince Lateef Fagbemi, SAN, said the early swearing-in of the tribunal judges was a clear demonstration of the judiciary’s commitment to ensuring that electoral disputes are handled promptly, competently and in accordance with the law. Fagbemi noted that election petition tribunals occupy a unique position in Nigeria’s democratic architecture, which is why the adjudication of electoral disputes continues to attract intense public attention and scrutiny. By providing the constitutional mechanism through which electoral grievances are peacefully resolved, he said, the tribunals are indispensable to political stability and public trust in the electoral process. The AGF drew attention to the far-reaching reforms introduced by the Electoral Act 2026, which he said aim to strengthen electoral transparency, promote internal party democracy, modernise electoral administration and redefine the framework for electoral disputes. The Act restricts judicial intervention in internal party affairs. Section 83(5) ousts the jurisdiction of the courts over disputes concerning the internal affairs of political parties, while Section 83(6) stipulates sanctions for intra-party litigation. The Act restricts interim and interlocutory injunctions in prohibited intra-party proceedings, provides for accelerated hearings, and prescribes minimum costs of N10 million each against the litigant and counsel. Likewise, Section 138(1) limits the grounds for election petitions. The amended law confines election petitions to corrupt practices, substantial non-compliance with electoral law, and failure to secure a majority of lawful votes. Significantly, it omits candidate disqualification as an express post-election ground, potentially shifting qualification disputes to pre-election proceedings. The AGF argued that the innovations in the amended Act represent a significant recalibration of Nigeria’s electoral framework ahead of the general elections. “Their ultimate transformative impact will depend on effective enforcement by INEC, compliance by political parties and judicial interpretation,” he added. For the INEC Chairman, Prof. Joash Amupitan, SAN, electoral litigation has become increasingly complex. He observed that, beyond the familiar questions of voting, counting and collation, disputes now concern voter accreditation, electronic transmission of results, technological failures, the integrity of digital records, party primaries, candidate nominations and the conduct of election officials. He said the Electoral Act 2026 has provided the legislative framework for the forthcoming general elections. “Of particular relevance is Section 60(3), which addresses electronic transmission of polling-unit results and the legal implications of communication failures. “Its interpretation, alongside other provisions of the new Act, may feature prominently in future petitions. “The deployment of the BVAS and the INEC Result Viewing Portal (IReV) has brought greater technological sophistication to election administration and public access to electoral information. “At the same time, these systems raise questions about the authenticity, admissibility and probative value of electronic records, their relationship with physical documents, and the consequences of technical disruptions. “A clear distinction must be maintained between the generation of technological information, the statutory purpose it serves and the legal standard required to prove a case before a tribunal. “The distinction between pre-election matters and post-election petitions must be carefully observed,” the INEC Chairman added. Although INEC and the judiciary perform distinct but complementary constitutional functions, the credibility of the elections cannot be judged solely by the conduct of voting or the declaration of results. It will also depend on public confidence that electoral disputes will be determined independently, fairly and in accordance with the law. As the CJN pointed out, the 2027 elections will be a defining moment in the nation’s democratic journey. She warned that the courtroom must not become an extension of the political arena, stressing that disputes must be resolved on the basis of the pleadings, evidence and applicable law. Of the 375 judges nominated, 138 have previous tribunal experience, while 237 are new to such proceedings. The workshop is expected to have equipped them with the skills and knowledge to navigate the murky waters of election litigation and arrive at legally sound decisions. By fairly determining any disputes arising from the 2027 elections, the judiciary stands to safeguard the people’s mandate, uphold constitutional supremacy and sustain public confidence in democratic governance. The post 2027 Elections: Beyond INEC, 375 Judges’ integrity under trial appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Gbenga Omotoso at 65: A rare gift of generosity and mentorship
item.description: By ROBERT UWEMEDIMO When Debbi Fields observed that “there is no such thing as coincidence; people come into our lives for a reason,” she captured a truth I have come to know profoundly through my relationship with Mr. Gbenga Omotoso. As he turned 65 on November 11, 2026, I pause to reflect on the extraordinary journey of more than two decades I have been privileged to share with the man I call boss – one who has been to me a father, mentor, benefactor, teacher, and, above all, a blessing from God Almighty. April 21, 2004, marked the beginning of a journey that would forever alter the course of my life. As I approached the wine-coloured plywood door on the second floor of a six-storey building at Ijora Causeway, Lagos – then the headquarters of The Comet newspaper – I opened it and found myself face to face with Mr. Omotoso, the Daily Editor, who needed someone to run errands for his office. He asked my name. “Robert,” I replied. “When will you resume work?” he asked. I was stunned. Here stood a man offering me a job before I had even applied; no interview, no credentials to present, no long queue outside a human resources office. Just one simple question that would rewrite the course of my life. “Tomorrow, sir,” I answered. That brief exchange marked the beginning of a relationship that shaped my life in ways I could never have imagined. I was a young boy who had lost his father at twelve. Little did I know that God was preparing another father figure for me in the person of Mr. Omotoso. When The Comet closed in 2006, a deep and overwhelming sense of uncertainty settled over us. Yet Mr. Omotoso looked me in the eye and assured me that wherever his career took him next, I would not be left behind. True to his word, when The Nation newspaper launched on July 31, 2006, I continued working with him as a 16-year-old boy. One quality that set him apart from the very beginning was his uncommon, almost instinctive generosity. I remember one particular week when he repeatedly asked whether I had eaten. Each time, he would give me some money for food. As time passed and his instinctive generosity continued, I grew uncomfortable and began answering, “Yes, sir, I have eaten,” not because I had suddenly become rich, but because I did not want him to think I was turning hunger into a business strategy. That is Mr. Omotoso. His kindness is never calculated; it flows naturally. His generosity was never limited to me. I recall a difficult period when the newspaper’s salaries were delayed for months. The newsroom was dampened, heavy with frustration. Sensing and discerning the quiet despair of his colleagues, he reached into his own pocket and gave everyone money to ease the hardship. That single gesture taught me a lesson I have never forgotten: true leadership is not about occupying an office; it is about lifting others when life weighs them down. item.dc:creator: Emmanuel Okogba
item.content:encoded: By ROBERT UWEMEDIMO When Debbi Fields observed that “there is no such thing as coincidence; people come into our lives for a reason,” she captured a truth I have come to know profoundly through my relationship with Mr. Gbenga Omotoso. As he turned 65 on November 11, 2026, I pause to reflect on the extraordinary journey of more than two decades I have been privileged to share with the man I call boss – one who has been to me a father, mentor, benefactor, teacher, and, above all, a blessing from God Almighty. April 21, 2004, marked the beginning of a journey that would forever alter the course of my life. As I approached the wine-coloured plywood door on the second floor of a six-storey building at Ijora Causeway, Lagos – then the headquarters of The Comet newspaper – I opened it and found myself face to face with Mr. Omotoso, the Daily Editor, who needed someone to run errands for his office. He asked my name. “Robert,” I replied. “When will you resume work?” he asked. I was stunned. Here stood a man offering me a job before I had even applied; no interview, no credentials to present, no long queue outside a human resources office. Just one simple question that would rewrite the course of my life. “Tomorrow, sir,” I answered. That brief exchange marked the beginning of a relationship that shaped my life in ways I could never have imagined. I was a young boy who had lost his father at twelve. Little did I know that God was preparing another father figure for me in the person of Mr. Omotoso. When The Comet closed in 2006, a deep and overwhelming sense of uncertainty settled over us. Yet Mr. Omotoso looked me in the eye and assured me that wherever his career took him next, I would not be left behind. True to his word, when The Nation newspaper launched on July 31, 2006, I continued working with him as a 16-year-old boy. One quality that set him apart from the very beginning was his uncommon, almost instinctive generosity. I remember one particular week when he repeatedly asked whether I had eaten. Each time, he would give me some money for food. As time passed and his instinctive generosity continued, I grew uncomfortable and began answering, “Yes, sir, I have eaten,” not because I had suddenly become rich, but because I did not want him to think I was turning hunger into a business strategy. That is Mr. Omotoso. His kindness is never calculated; it flows naturally. His generosity was never limited to me. I recall a difficult period when the newspaper’s salaries were delayed for months. The newsroom was dampened, heavy with frustration. Sensing and discerning the quiet despair of his colleagues, he reached into his own pocket and gave everyone money to ease the hardship. That single gesture taught me a lesson I have never forgotten: true leadership is not about occupying an office; it is about lifting others when life weighs them down. Beyond feeding my body, Mr. Omotoso fed my dreams. He encouraged me to keep studying while working and never once treated my academic ambitions as an inconvenience. During one management meeting, when questions were raised about my qualifications, he defended my potential and appealed for patience while I worked toward becoming a graduate. I was determined not to disappoint him. In 2014, I graduated from the then Lagos State Polytechnic with a Distinction. He celebrated the achievement, then immediately urged me to aim higher. With his continued support, I went on to Caleb University, Imota, Lagos, where I earned a Bachelor of Science degree in Computer Science in 2019, graduating with Second Class Upper honours and a CGPA of 4.36. For someone who had started as an errand boy, this was more than academic progress. It was living proof that when someone believes in your potential, your circumstances need not determine your destination. Mr. Omotoso’s fatherly role extended far beyond the professional and academic. When I married in 2018, he provided a Honda Pilot and a personal driver to take me around all day, ensuring the occasion was memorable. On August 20, 2019, he was appointed Lagos State Commissioner for Information and Strategy. Before leaving The Nation, he ensured my contributions were recognised with a promotion to Web Officer. A month into his new assignment, he invited me to join him at the Ministry of Information and Strategy. That invitation opened yet another significant chapter in my career. Since then, I have had the privilege of serving closely with him as his Personal Assistant and Programme Analyst within the Lagos State Government. His commitment to my progress did not end there. He played an instrumental role in my appointment to the Lagos State Civil Service on December 31, 2024, personally presenting my credentials to Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu for consideration and approval. How does one adequately thank a man who has consistently opened doors, sometimes long before one even knew those doors existed? Yet my story is only one among countless testimonies of his compassion. Over the years, I have watched him discreetly pay hospital bills for people with whom he shares no family ties, sponsor the education of children whose parents could not afford school fees, and quietly rescue others from difficult circumstances. He does not need a camera to demonstrate kindness, nor does he wait for applause before helping others. Behind his serious editorial background and the demands of public office is also a man blessed with a remarkable sense of humour. An accomplished journalist, columnist and writer, Mr. Omotoso has a gift for satire. His humorous observations can turn even tense moments into shared laughter. And then there is table tennis. Anyone who has faced him across the table knows that losing is not exactly his favourite pastime. He approaches every game with the intensity of an editor scrutinising a controversial front-page headline. Every point matters, every rally is a battle, and every defeat deserves a detailed explanation. At 65, I suspect his opponents will still need more than youthful energy to defeat him. As I celebrate this remarkable man, I see far beyond the professional titles and accomplishments. I see a compassionate father figure, a bridge-builder, a generous leader, and a man whose quiet influence continues to transform lives. Sir, on your 65th birthday, I pray that Almighty God grants you long life, sound health, renewed strength, divine protection, and enduring peace. May the years ahead be filled with greater accomplishments, happiness, and the joy of seeing the many lives you have touched continue to flourish. May God reward every sacrifice you have made for others, replenish every resource you have so freely and generously shared, and surround you with love, honour and abundant blessings. May your pen never run dry, your wisdom never diminish, your laughter never cease, and may you continue winning your table tennis matches, even when your opponents believe they deserve a chance! For more than 22 years, I have experienced your kindness firsthand. I may never be able to repay all you have done for me, but I will forever remain grateful. Happy 65th birthday, my boss, my mentor, my father figure, and my God-sent benefactor. The world may know you as Gbenga Omotoso, the accomplished journalist and Commissioner. I know you as the man God used to rewrite the story of a fatherless boy. And for that, I will remain eternally grateful. •Uwemedimo is a Programme Analyst and Personal Assistant to the Lagos State Commissioner for Information and Strategy. The post Gbenga Omotoso at 65: A rare gift of generosity and mentorship appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Women and their househelps: The cruelty must stop
item.description: By Fred Chukwuelobe I don’t mind being called a misogynist or accused of generalising on this matter. Frankly, I think we have reached a point where somebody has to speak out loudly against the inhuman treatment some Igbo women mete out to their domestic servants. And while we are at it, we must also call out their husbands, particularly those who watch helplessly as their wives turn other people’s children into household slaves. Some of these men are either complicit or simply too weak to call their wives to order. For quite some time now, stories of Igbo women who mercilessly maltreat their domestic servants have been making the rounds. The latest is the disturbing incident in Ogidi, Anambra State, where a woman allegedly beat her 10-year-old domestic servant so mercilessly that a neighbour had to intervene to rescue the child. Reports identified the girl as Chizoba Ifeanyi and the alleged perpetrator as her aunt, Mrs Adaobi Agbonta. The incident reportedly occurred because the little girl refused to sweep the house. Imagine that! What manner of woman beats a ten-year-old child to that extent over an ordinary household chore? What exactly does she expect from a child of that age? And what would have happened if that neighbour had not intervened? Unfortunately, this is not the first time we have heard such stories. In July 2020, Nigerians were horrified by the story of 10-year-old Nneoma Nnadi in Enugu. Her employer, Ifeoma Ozougwu, was accused of inserting a six-inch nail into the child’s skull, using hot pressing irons on her body and subjecting her to other forms of torture. Her husband was also arrested in connection with the incident. It was one of those stories that made one wonder whether some people were actually human beings. In May 2023, another case emerged from Nkpor, Anambra State, involving an eight-year-old househelp who was allegedly brutally beaten by her employer, Chinyere Ifesinachi. The child reportedly sustained multiple injuries. Then there was the March 2018 case in Lagos involving a woman, Nkeiruka Ngwu, who was arrested for allegedly using a hot pressing iron and hot water on her 10-year-old househelp, Chioma Samuel, a child reportedly brought from Abia State after the death of her father. These are just some of the reported cases. And before anybody accuses me of deliberately picking on Igbo women, let me acknowledge that similar incidents have occurred in other parts of the country. In March 2026, Premium Times reported the arrest of a woman in Cross River State over the alleged assault of her five-year-old niece, who was reportedly being used as a domestic helper. In Delta State, a woman was sentenced to two years’ imprisonment in 2020 for using a hot kitchen knife to disfigure the mouth of her nine-year-old housemaid. I am not aware of any reliable national statistics establishing which ethnic group records the highest number of such abuses. But the frequency of disturbing stories involving women in our part of the c

In Delta State, a woman was sentenced to two years’ imprisonment in 2020 for using a hot kitchen knife to disfigure the mouth of her nine-year-old housemaid. I am not aware of any reliable national statistics establishing which ethnic group records the highest number of such abuses. But the frequency of disturbing stories involving women in our part of the country should worry us. We cannot continue pretending that nothing is happening. Thank goodness I am Igbo, so nobody should waste time accusing me of Igbophobia. I am talking about a problem that deserves to be confronted within our society. And I am certainly not suggesting that all Igbo women behave this way. Far from it. There are countless decent, compassionate and responsible Igbo women who treat their domestic workers with love and dignity. But those who engage in these atrocities must be called out. What exactly is the matter with some of these women? Why are they so wicked to other people’s children? These are children born to poor parents, just as their own children were born. Some have lost their parents. Others come from homes where their parents cannot afford to provide for them. They are sent to live with relatives or brought into households where they are expected to receive care, assistance and, in some cases, an opportunity to go to school. Instead, some end up living like slaves. They are made to wake up before everybody else, cook, wash, clean, fetch water, look after babies and perform virtually every household chore. They eat last, sleep last and are often the first to be blamed whenever anything goes wrong. Some are fed with leftovers or denied food altogether for the slightest offence. Others are denied access to education and decent clothing. Once you see some of these women and their children on an outing to events and even church services, you can easily identify the househelp. The difference in their dressing alone tells a story. The madam’s children are beautifully dressed, while the little girl or boy accompanying them looks like somebody picked up from the street. I recall seeing a woman who took her children to a fast-food restaurant. While the children sat comfortably at the table enjoying their lunch, their domestic servant sat somewhere nearby, clutching madam’s handbag and watching them eat. She was not even treated as someone who deserved to sit at the same table and enjoy a meal. I found the sight particularly disturbing. I also recall a case in which a woman allegedly used a hot pressing iron on her domestic servant because the child drank a soft drink meant for her own children. A bottle of soft drink! Can you imagine burning another person’s child because she drank what your children were meant to drink? What kind of wickedness is that? Some of these women apparently believe that because they provide accommodation and food for their domestic servants, they have acquired ownership of their lives. They forget that these children have parents, feelings, dignity and rights. Even if their parents are dead, they remain human beings deserving of compassion. And what is even more disturbing is that some of these women are regular churchgoers. They attend services, participate in church activities, make donations and sometimes occupy prominent positions in their religious organisations. On Sundays, they sing praises and pray fervently. But when they return home, the same hands that are raised in worship are used to beat and torment another person’s child. What manner of Christianity is that? Then there are the husbands. I have a special word for them. Some of you need to grow a backbone. How can you sit in your living room, know that your wife is beating and maltreating a little child, and pretend that nothing is happening? Is the child not a human being? Does your responsibility to protect the vulnerable end because the person abusing the child happens to be your wife? Marriage does not require you to surrender your conscience. If your wife is cruel to a domestic servant, call her to order. If she refuses to change, protect the child and involve the appropriate authorities. Do not become an accomplice simply because you want peace at home. I also have a word for the relatives who send their children away to live with wealthy relations. Please, do not abandon your parental responsibilities simply because somebody has promised to take care of your child. Visit. Call. Ask questions. Find out what the child eats, where the child sleeps and whether the child is attending school. Do not wait until the child returns home with scars or ends up in a hospital before you realise that something has gone terribly wrong. WE MUST DECLARE WAR ON THIS PRACTICE. I believe it is time for Igbo sociocultural organisations, town unions, women’s organisations, civil society groups and religious institutions to take this matter seriously. It should no longer be treated as an ordinary domestic disagreement. Where are our women organisations? Where are the church groups that organise meetings every week? Where are the Christian Mothers’ organisations? Where are the wives of our governors? Why should we wait until another child is nearly killed before everybody starts issuing statements? The First Ladies of the South-East states should take up this challenge and champion a regional campaig

item.description: By Chimaobi Nwaiwu NNEWI — South-East governors have been urged to support and patronise factories and companies established by indigenes of the zone to generate employment, tackle insecurity and unemployment, and accelerate regional development. The Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Audi Company Limited, Dr Clem Ifezue, made the call in an exclusive interview with Vanguard in Awka, Anambra State. Ifezue, an Anambra-born industrialist, said indigenous industries had the capacity to provide jobs for thousands of unemployed people and contribute significantly to the economic growth of the South-East if given adequate government support and patronage. He said Audi Company Limited was a technical products and services marketing company registered in Nigeria, with a vision to assemble leading global brands and make them readily available to Nigerians. According to him, the company has been operating for over 20 years, with branches across the country’s regions, including Enugu, and partnerships with several local and international companies. Highlighting areas where South-East governors could partner with the company, Ifezue said its operations covered automobile assembly, power solutions, marine logistics and engineering works. According to him, the company has been operating for over 20 years, with branches across the country’s regions, including Enugu, and partnerships with several local and international companies. Highlighting areas where South-East governors could partner with the company, Ifezue said its operations covered automobile assembly, power solutions, marine logistics and engineering works. He explained that the company’s power solutions included generators powered by Perkins and York engines of British origin, as well as solar systems, hybrid inverters, lithium batteries and solar panels. “When I say power solution, it means that we have our own brand of generators, using Perkins and York engines, both of United Kingdom origin. “We have been in existence for a while and Nigerians have been enjoying the quality of our products and can attest to that. “We have our own brand of solar system, we have our inverter which is hybrid, we have our battery which is lithium and we have our solar panels, with well-trained engineers and technicians working for us. We are a big employer of labour,” he said. On marine logistics, Ifezue said the company had partnerships in boat construction and the provision of marine facilities for transportation, fishing and movement of goods, among other applications. He also disclosed that the company was involved in engineering and construction projects for state governments and private individuals. Ifezue, who is also the Director-General of the Mines Crafts Registered Association of Nigeria, said South-East governors could leverage the company’s expertise to attract investments and accelerate infrastructure development in the region. The former General Manager of John Holt Plc lamented the difficulties of establishing and sustaining businesses in Nigeria, attributing some of the challenges to what he described as inadequate government emphasis on supporting indigenous enterprises. He said local companies often competed with foreign operators who had limited investments and business establishments in Nigeria but were still able to secure contracts and patronage. “We compete with a lot of people who do not have anything here in Nigeria, people who just come with one briefcase, do business and go, but we are established here. “That is why we said we represent the best brands. Together with Mikano Motors, we assemble cars, sell and maintain the cars in Nigeria,” he said. He acknowledged the Federal Government’s efforts to reduce high bank interest rates, but argued that more deliberate policies were needed to enable indigenous companies to compete effectively and provide quality products at affordable prices. According to him, government remains the biggest spender in Nigeria through its activities at the federal, state and local government levels and could significantly influence the growth of local industries through its procurement decisions. He cited the purchase of official vehicles, equipment for government agencies and vehicles for public officers as areas where governments could patronise locally assembled products. Ifezue also referenced the Ebonyi State Government’s provision of vehicles to doctors serving in rural communities as an example of how government procurement could support public service delivery and local businesses. “If government is sincere with their preaching of patronising Made-in-Nigeria goods, it will be a good thing for the economy. “It is by so doing that our competitors will begin to think of setting up plants here, but as far as the government is ignoring indigenous companies and patronising those that are not established here, that campaign will not be successful,” he said. He urged governments at all levels to extend their patronage beyond automobile assembly plants to other products manufactured locally, arguing that such a policy would stimulate investment, create employment and strengthen the economy. Ifezue expressed optimism that a coordinated partnership between South-East governors and indigenous businesses would encourage more investors to establish factories in the region. “If the South-East governors can come together and form an alliance with us, more industries will be attracted and located here, our people will be employed and more development will come. “Location of industries goes with numbers. If we are assured of high patronage, more people will set up factories and our people stand to gain. No investor will like to invest where he cannot make a profit,” he said. item.title: Right-sizing the map of Africa
item.description: The United Nations General Assembly has, for the first time, formally endorsed a global shift away from the centuries-old Mercator map in favour of projections that show Africa—and other equatorial regions—in their true relative size. This “Correct the Map” resolution, spearheaded by Togo on behalf of the African Group and backed by the African Union, passed by 164 votes to one, with six abstentions. While non-binding, it marks a watershed moment in how the world visually represents the continent—and, by extension, how it perceives Africa’s weight in global affairs. The root of the misrepresentation lies in the Mercator projection, devised in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator for maritime navigation. To keep compass bearings straight, Mercator preserved angles and shapes—but at the cost of area. The result: landmasses near the poles, such as Europe, North America and Greenland, are visually enlarged, while those near the equator, including Africa, Latin America and South Asia, are shrunk. On typical Mercator wall maps, Greenland appears roughly the same size as Africa. In reality, Africa covers about 30.3 million square kilometres, making it around 14 times larger than Greenland’s 2.1 million square kilometres. This is not a minor quirk; it is a systematic visual bias baked into the most widely used world map for nearly five centuries. The resolution encourages governments, schools, international organisations, media houses and technology companies to adopt equal-area projections, especially the Equal Earth projection, whenever comparative continental size matters. It frames map distortion as more than a technical issue—calling it a cognitive, educational, cultural and geopolitical problem that has contributed to the symbolic minimisation of Africa in the global imagination. While symbolic correction matters, Africa’s greatest vulnerabilities lie in structural exploitation and escalating insecurity, notably from Islamist insurgencies across the Sahel, Lake Chad Basin and parts of the Horn. Map reform must be paired with hard-edged action on multiple fronts. First, curb external exploitation and illicit financial flows by tightening transparency on extractives, choking illicit financial flows through cross-border tax cooperation, and rebalancing investment terms to prioritise local content and value addition. Second, confront Islamist insecurity with a whole-of-system approach by funding and professionalising regional forces, targeting financing networks that fuel insurgencies, investing in governance at the frontier, and countering extremist narratives through community engagement. Third, lock in development dividends that undercut recruitment by expanding vocational training and agro-processing corridors tied to the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), funding climate-resilient livelihoods, and prioritising children’s education and primary healthcare. item.dc:creator: Emmanuel Okogba
item.content:encoded: The United Nations General Assembly has, for the first time, formally endorsed a global shift away from the centuries-old Mercator map in favour of projections that show Africa—and other equatorial regions—in their true relative size. The root of the misrepresentation lies in the Mercator projection, devised in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator for maritime navigation. To keep compass bearings straight, Mercator preserved angles and shapes—but at the cost of area. The result: landmasses near the poles, such as Europe, North America and Greenland, are visually enlarged, while those near the equator, including Africa, Latin America and South Asia, are shrunk. On typical Mercator wall maps, Greenland appears roughly the same size as Africa. In reality, Africa covers about 30.3 million square kilometres, making it around 14 times larger than Greenland’s 2.1 million square kilometres. This is not a minor quirk; it is a systematic visual bias baked into the most widely used world map for nearly five centuries. The resolution encourages governments, schools, international organisations, media houses and technology companies to adopt equal-area projections, especially the Equal Earth projection, whenever comparative continental size matters. It frames map distortion as more than a technical issue—calling it a cognitive, educational, cultural and geopolitical problem that has contributed to the symbolic minimisation of Africa in the global imagination. While symbolic correction matters, Africa’s greatest vulnerabilities lie in structural exploitation and escalating insecurity, notably from Islamist insurgencies across the Sahel, Lake Chad Basin and parts of the Horn. Map reform must be paired with hard-edged action on multiple fronts. First, curb external exploitation and illicit financial flows by tightening transparency on extractives, choking illicit financial flows through cross-border tax cooperation, and rebalancing investment terms to prioritise local content and value addition. Second, confront Islamist insecurity with a whole-of-system approach by funding and professionalising regional forces, targeting financing networks that fuel insurgencies, investing in governance at the frontier, and countering extremist narratives through community engagement. Third, lock in development dividends that undercut recruitment by expanding vocational training and agro-processing corridors tied to the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), funding climate-resilient livelihoods, and prioritising children’s education and primary healthcare. Fourth, reform global governance to reflect Africa’s weight by pressing for permanent African seats at the UN Security Council. The UN’s “Correct the Map” resolution is a necessary correction of a 450-year-old visual injustice. But maps alone do not feed children, stop bullets or reclaim stolen wealth. item.title: Some PFAS chemicals are declining in English rivers but others are appearing
item.description: The River Wye in Derbyshire, England Dave Porter/Alamy The concentration of two of the most well-studied PFAS forever chemicals are showing a strong downward trend in English rivers. The finding adds to a mixed story for the power of global restrictions. The levels of perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) and perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) in English rivers have fallen by 30 per cent and 29 per cent, respectively, over the past decade, according to a new report by scientists at the Environment Agency (EA) , a UK government green regulator. Both of these human-made chemicals take a long time to break down in the environment. The International Agency for Research on Cancer recently designated PFOA as carcinogenic to humans , and both forever chemicals have been linked to reproductive health and developmental impacts as well as other serious health issues. Advertisement Read more Fish-based pet food may expose cats and dogs to forever chemicals Under the United Nations Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants, the use of PFOS was restricted from 2009, and the use of PFOA was restricted from 2019 – although there were country-specific caveats on which uses they applied to. They had both been used in non-stick coatings on consumer products as well as in industrial processes. Both were also used in firefighting foams, a major source of PFAS pollution entering the environment, with a ban on PFOA in firefighting foams only coming into force in the UK in 2025. Rob Bradburne , the EA’s chief scientist, describes his group’s results as proof that the global ban was “a really positive move”. But, he adds that the huge range of PFAS chemicals is going to “complicate the story”. An issue that is clear in the dataset for England is that while these two main PFAS have declined, many other “forever chemicals” that are being used to replace them – such as short-chain PFAS and fluorotelomer compounds – have now emerged in the environment at detectable levels. Free newsletter Sign up to The Earth Edition Sign up to newsletter There are around 10,000 chemicals defined as PFAS, and they are used in a huge range of products and processes, from cosmetics to industrial lubricants. But the health and environmental impacts of many of these chemicals are relatively understudied. One of the short-chain PFAS that is now particularly widespread across the world is trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) – which can form when pesticides, refrigerants and pharmaceuticals break down in the environment. The EA report confirmed that TFA is widespread in England, and a separate study published this week confirmed that it is also widespread across the UK more generally. “These findings add to the growing weight of evidence that PFAS pollution must be tackled at source if we are to protect our environment and our health,” says Hannah Evans , who worked on this second study and works with the UK environmental charity Fidra. “Other countries are already progressing towards this end… The UK
item.dc:creator: Shosha Adie
item.content:encoded: The River Wye in Derbyshire, England Dave Porter/Alamy The concentration of two of the most well-studied PFAS forever chemicals are showing a strong downward trend in English rivers. The finding adds to a mixed story for the power of global restrictions. The levels of perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) and perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) in English rivers have fallen by 30 per cent and 29 per cent, respectively, over the past decade, according to a new report by scientists at the Environment Agency (EA) , a UK government green regulator. Both of these human-made chemicals take a long time to break down in the environment. The International Agency for Research on Cancer recently designated PFOA as carcinogenic to humans , and both forever chemicals have been linked to reproductive health and developmental impacts as well as other serious health issues. Advertisement Read more Fish-based pet food may expose cats and dogs to forever chemicals Under the United Nations Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants, the use of PFOS was restricted from 2009, and the use of PFOA was restricted from 2019 – although there were country-specific caveats on which uses they applied to. They had both been used in non-stick coatings on consumer products as well as in industrial processes. Both were also used in firefighting foams, a major source of PFAS pollution entering the environment, with a ban on PFOA in firefighting foams only coming into force in the UK in 2025. Rob Bradburne , the EA’s chief scientist, describes his group’s results as proof that the global ban was “a really positive move”. But, he adds that the huge range of PFAS chemicals is going to “complicate the story”. An issue that is clear in the dataset for England is that while these two main PFAS have declined, many other “forever chemicals” that are being used to replace them – such as short-chain PFAS and fluorotelomer compounds – have now emerged in the environment at detectable levels. Free newsletter Sign up to The Earth Edition Sign up to newsletter There are around 10,000 chemicals defined as PFAS, and they are used in a huge range of products and processes, from cosmetics to industrial lubricants. But the health and environmental impacts of many of these chemicals are relatively understudied. One of the short-chain PFAS that is now particularly widespread across the world is trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) – which can form when pesticides, refrigerants and pharmaceuticals break down in the environment. The EA report confirmed that TFA is widespread in England, and a separate study published this week confirmed that it is also widespread across the UK more generally. “These findings add to the growing weight of evidence that PFAS pollution must be tackled at source if we are to protect our environment and our health,” says Hannah Evans , who worked on this second study and works with the UK environmental charity Fidra. “Other countries are already progressing towards this end… The UK cannot afford to fall further behind,” says Evans. Read more Wastewater treatment plants funnel PFAS into drinking water Currently, the EU is looking at a blanket ban on all PFAS chemicals, so that when specific chemicals are prohibited they aren’t simply replaced by another PFAS that may also eventually be identified as harmful and persistent in the environment. The UK government has said it is following this closely but has given no timescales on when a similar policy might be introduced. Alistair Boxall at the University of York, UK, says that the decline in legacy pollutants and increase in short-chain replacements was observed in a recently published European-wide monitoring study he took part in. He believes the change shows why bans that target the entire group of chemicals could offer a better way forward. “We seem to always be playing catch-up with chemicals like PFAS, so need to be much more agile in the way that we monitor and manage these substances. The idea of using grouping approaches could help,” says Boxall. Patrick Byrne at Liverpool John Moores University, UK, says that the grouping approach is useful and something that scientists have argued strongly for. Plant biology provides inspiration for PFAS replacement Forever chemicals are renowned for their durability and their non-stick properties, but they persist for years in the environment. An alternative inspired by plants doesn’t have the same problem He also says that the story isn’t over for PFOS and PFOA. Though they are decreasing globally, it’s important to remember they are still highly persistent and found in almost every water body. The levels of PFOS being recorded are still, in many cases, higher than the UK and EU Environmental Quality Standard, which is set to reflect the concentration above which the chemical will affect ecosystems. Currently, PFOS is the only individual PFAS with such a standard in England, but others are under development . “This report adds to our growing understanding of how PFAS enter our environment, but we must not wait for a complete picture before acting,” says Chloe Alexander , a campaigner at Wildlife and Countryside Link, an umbrella organisation in the UK that brings together many volunteer and charitable groups. “History is full of late lessons from early warnings, where ignored science allowed preventable harm to become widespread and, in some cases, irreversible,” says Alexander. “The longer it waits, the greater the risks to people and wildlife – and the higher the costs of clean-up and toxic waste disposal.”

item.title: Democrat Scott Colom wins historic Senate race in Mississippi
item.description: Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi after a final count on Wednesday, becoming the state's first Black US senator since Reconstruction. His narrow victory adds to the Democrats' midterm gains as President Donald Trump's party suffers a series of defeats.

item.title: Pope Leo XIV returns to second homeland Peru to a nationwide welcome
item.description: Pope Leo XIV arrived in Peru on Wednesday for the final leg of his South American tour, returning to the country where he spent more than two decades as a missionary and bishop. Thousands gathered to welcome him home as “Padre Robert”, with many hoping his visit will bring attention to poverty, crime and political instability.

item.title: CEO Jensen Huang's job is suddenly on the line at Nvidia
item.description: Nvidia’s board is set to decide the future of its founder Jensen Huang after revelations that he had a romantic relationship with a company executive, days after it emerged that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The board held urgent talks on Wednesday night after news broke of the Nvidia chief executive’s relationship with Kimberly Powell, the chipmaker’s vice-president of healthcare, according to people familiar with the matter. The relationship with an Nvidia employee deepens an already damaging scandal for the $4.2 trillion semiconductor group. Huang on Sunday admitted to having an affair, two days after the FT reported his romantic links to an executive at an Nvidia client, who US officials believe is a Chinese intelligence asset. Read full article Comments

item.title: Olumide Oworu Declares House of Representatives Bid for Surulere Constituency 1 in 2027
item.description: Olumide Oworu has declared his candidacy for the Federal House of Representatives to represent Surulere Constituency 1 in 2027. Photo Credit: Olumide Oworu/Instagram Actor and media personality Olumide Oworu has declared his intention to contest for the Federal House of Representatives seat for Surulere Constituency 1 in the 2027 general elections. He will be running under the platform of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM). Olumide, who grew up in Surulere, Lagos, has a long-standing connection to the constituency. He began his acting career as a child, appearing in television productions such as Everyday People , before gaining wider recognition for his role in The Johnsons and other Nigerian film and television projects. This is his second attempt to enter legislative politics. In 2023, he declared his intention to contest for a seat in the Lagos State House of Assembly under the Labour Party. However, administrative challenges prevented his name from appearing on the final ballot. Olumide Oworu’s official campaign poster for the House of Representatives seat representing Surulere Constituency 1 under the Allied Peoples Movement. Photo Credit: Olumide Oworu/Instagram Reflecting on that experience in his candidacy announcement on Instagram, Olumide said the support he received from young people in Surulere had strengthened his belief in their readiness for more active participation in governance. “Despite the administrative hurdles that left our names off the final ballot, your resilience showed me that our vision was never a passing phase. Instead, it was the beginning of something much more significant,” he wrote. Explaining his decision to contest again, this time for a seat in the House of Representatives, he added: “We cannot afford to sit on the sidelines while our future is decided by a political class that won’t have to live with the consequences of today’s choices.” His campaign has highlighted issues including gaps in public services, community infrastructure and the participation of young Nigerians in policy decisions. Announcing his candidacy, he said he looked forward to continued support as he and his supporters worked towards what he described as a mission to “Reset Nigeria”. Olumide Oworu is contesting for a legislative seat in Surulere Constituency 1 under the APM platform. item.title: Spain coach optimistic over Yamal’s fitness for England Nations League clash
item.description: Spain coach Luis de la Fuente said Wednesday he is optimistic Barcelona winger Lamine Yamal will be fit to face England in the Nations League at the weekend. The 19-year-old winger will miss the world champions’ visit to face the Czech Republic in Prague on Thursday with a knee problem and is set to join up with Spain after that game. Yamal played for Barcelona in the 2-1 La Liga win over Atletico Madrid on Sunday and on Monday Spain said he would not travel to face the Czechs. “He got hurt in the last match, he had some discomfort in one knee, he went for the usual treatment, a scan in Barcelona, and they saw he had inflammation and fluid in the knee — that meant he needed rest,” De la Fuente told reporters. “Our medical staff and his medical staff have a fantastic relationship, and I decided that his trip here should be avoided without knowing whether he’d be in any condition to play.” The coach said he had spoken to the winger and his recovery was looking positive ahead of England’s visit to Madrid on Sunday. “He’s doing a series of exercises with his physio and with the club that indicate the recovery is going well,” continued De la Fuente. “We believe, I’m optimistic, that on Friday he’ll be with us.” De la Fuente dismissed the idea that Yamal, who came third in the Ballon d’Or voting in October, has any special privileges compared to his La Roja team-mates. “He has no privileges, and his team-mates are relaxed about it, because we treat everyone the same,” added the coach. “In similar situations we would have done exactly the same for any other player, and the players know that.” – Unstoppable run – Spain have won all four games so far in Group A3 and sealed qualification to the quarter-finals. De la Fuente’s side are unbeaten in their last 43 competitive outings, and the coach said it provided his team with extra motivation. “We want to keep setting new milestones, and this is another one,” explained De la Fuente. “None of us would probably ever have thought we’d even reach 35, because we already felt those were astronomical numbers, but having reached 43, you think, my goodness, we want to get to 44, of course we do.” Spain won their previous outing away in Croatia with a brace from Arsenal’s Mikel Merino. The midfielder is frequently used as a substitute by De la Fuente to great effect, with Merino netting vital goals against Portugal and Belgium in the World Cup off the bench this summer. Merino said he would like to be a starter for Spain but he would not kick up a fuss. “Of course, what player wouldn’t like to get (more) minutes?” Merino told reporters. “You’ll never hear me complain about the coach’s decision, I will respect it… but all players want to be important, have minutes and enjoy themselves on the pitch.” The post Spain coach optimistic over Yamal’s fitness for England Nations League clash appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Gadi Eisenkot unveils agenda to reverse Netanyahu’s policies
item.description: The bloc of Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot introduced a series of bills at the start of the legislative session that target Benjamin Netanyahu and his policies. They include launching an official government-led inquiry into the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, setting term limits on the position of prime minister and overturning changes the outgoing Netanyahu-led government made to limit the powers of the judiciary. FRANCE 24's Sharon Gaffney speaks with Rina Bassist, Editor at Al-Monitor.

item.title: DSS foils major terror plot, intercepts 21 AK-47s, other arms from Niger in Sokoto
item.description: By Soni Daniel, Northern Region Editor Barely 70 days to the the 2027 general elections, the Department of State Security Services has foiled a major terror plot by intercepting a large consignment of high-calibre weapons and ammunition smuggled into the country from Niger Republic. The weapons, including 21 AK-47 rifles, 4 PKT machine guns and 825 magazines, were intercepted exclusively by DSS officers in Dawakawa, Goronyo Local Government Area of Sokoto State, following intensive surveillance of terror cells seeking to transport deadly weapons into Nigeria ahead of the general elections. A security source disclosed that, given increased interception of illegal weapons by the DSS around the country, terror groups have turned to women and beasts of burden, particularly camels, to move illegal weapons into and around the country. It will be recalled that earlier in the week, DSS operatives in Talata Mafaran LGA of Zamfara State, arrested another suspected female arms courier, Hafsat Umar. Umar, who was arrested with 12 grenades and two ammunition belts, is the 14th female illegal arms courier arrested by the DSS between February 2025 and November 2026. Intelligence indicated that the suspected illegal arms courier travelled to Niger State to source ammunition for delivery to a notorious bandit leader, Saidu Marafa, who is based in Kani Kawa, Maradun LGA of Zamfara State. The arrests by the DSS span Zamfara, Nasarawa, Ebonyi, Taraba, Kaduna and Plateau States. Notable among the arrests was that of Aisha Mohammed, apprehended last month in Keffi, Nasarawa State, while allegedly conveying arms and ammunition through a notorious arms dealer and kidnapper simply called Sani. Recovered from Aisha were 202 rounds of 7.62mm AK-47 ammunition and three empty AK-47 magazines. In September, 2026, two female couriers, Chika Aguzie and Blessing Nwamba were arrested at separate locations in Ebonyi State over their alleged involvement in the supply of weapons and explosives to commanders of the outlawed Eastern Security Network (ESN). The commanders include Chinonso Amobi Okafor, aka Temple, and B44, reportedly based in Anambra State. 14 wraps of IED detonators, were recovered during the operation. In August, DSS arrested one Rabiatu Halidu, on Abacha Road, Katu LGA of Nasarawa State with 501 rounds of 7.62mm ammunition. In February, DSS officers arrested one Aisha Ibrahim in Tsafe, LGA of Zamfara State, with 975 rounds of ammunition. Arested in January were Sakina Muhammad and Badariyya Abubakar, along Wukari-Jalingo Road, Taraba State, with one AK-47 rifle, 984 rounds of special ammunition, 105 rounds of GPMG ammunition and 14 empty AK-47 magazines. The Service also recorded several arrests in 2025, including Rahane Sanusi, in Talatan Mafara LGA of Zamfara State. She was caught while conveying ammunition from an illegal arms dealer in Sokoto State to a notorious bandit, Ibrahim Bare, aka Baba, in Anka LGA of the state. Also arrested during the period was Suwaib
